item.title: Far-right AfD tops second state poll in Germany, chancellor Friedrich Merz faces uncertain future
item.description: Almost nobody expects him to lead the Christian Democratic Union into the next federal elections.
item.content:encoded:
Friedrich Merz’s demeanour was grim as he stepped before the cameras on Sunday evening to address his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party after two more disappointing state election results. Following what the German chancellor had called the CDU’s “worst defeat in many years” in Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago, Merz described the result of Sunday’s Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania election as a “disaster”.

His party won just 4.9% of the vote in the largely rural, eastern, coastal state. This means that, for the first time, it fell short of the 5% threshold needed for entering a state parliament.

The Christian Democratic Union found itself squeezed in a contest between the minister-president of the Social Democratic Party (SPD), Manuela Schwesig, and the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). As in Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD topped the poll but fell short of a majority.

Schwesig’s campaign was criticised for trying to unite all voters opposed to the AfD behind her and thus harming the chances of other parties. But complaining about political opponents trying to win over your supporters is hardly a compelling argument for the CDU.

In Berlin, the evening got worse for Merz. Exit polls suggested the party was on course for 20% there, but in the final count it slipped back to 18.8%. This represents a loss of 9.5 percentage points...

item.title: Court grants default bail to six Ukrainians arrested for suspected links with Myanmar armed groups
item.description: Although they had been arrested under UAPA, the NIA chargesheet accused them only of immigration offences.
item.content:encoded:
A Delhi court on Wednesday granted default bail to six Ukrainians who were arrested by the National Investigation Agency in March for allegedly having links to ethnic armed groups in Myanmar that are hostile to India, PTI reported.

Default bail is granted when an investigating agency fails to complete its probe and file a chargesheet within the statutory period while an accused is in custody.

On Friday, the court granted default bail to Matthew Aaron Van Dyke, a United States citizen who is also accused in the case.

The seven foreigners were allegedly involved in supplying weapons and military equipment to ethnic armed groups operating in Myanmar, as well as providing them with training.

On September 8, the NIA filed a chargesheet against them for illegally entering, staying and moving in India under the 2025 Immigration and Foreigners Act.

Although they had been arrested under the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act, the agency had only accused them of immigration violations in the chargesheet.

Special NIA Judge Prashant Sharma on Wednesday discharged the six Ukrainians under the Immigration and Foreigners Act, noting that the Foreigners Regional Registration Office had compounded the offences against them by imposing a fine of Rs 5.5 lakh on each, reported PTI.

item.title: Noida workers’ protest: SC stays Allahabad HC order quashing NSA detention of activist
item.description: Directives asking Gautam Buddha Nagar District Magistrate Medha Roopam to pay Rs 5 lakh as compensation to 25-year-old Akriti Chaudhary were also set aside.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Wednesday stayed the Allahabad High Court order that had quashed the National Security Act detention of a 25-year-old Delhi University graduate after the workers’ protest in Noida, reported Live Law.

A bench of Justices Satish Chandra Sharma and NK Singh also set aside the High Court’s direction to Gautam Buddha Nagar District Magistrate Medha Roopam to pay Rs 5 lakh as compensation from her salary to Akriti Chaudhary.

The video recording of the proceedings was muted by the court, and media access was blocked, reported Live Law.

On September 2, the High Court said that the compensation should be deducted from the salary of Roopam, who had passed the order to detain Chaudhary, and other officials responsible for enforcing it.

The detention order against Chaudhary was devoid of material evidence and was passed “without application of mind”, the High Court bench of Justices Atul Sreedharan and Achal Sachdev had said.

Chaudhary has been in jail for more than five months. She had been detained on April 11, two days before the protest in Noida turned violent, her family stated. In May, the Uttar Pradesh Police invoked the National Security Act against her while she was in custody.

item.title: Booker Prize 2026: Here are the opening lines of the six shortlisted novels
item.description: Of the shortlisted authors, Marlon James won the prize in 2015, and Douglas Stuart, in 2020. Elizabeth Strout has been shortlisted in 2022.
item.content:encoded:
The shortlist for the 2026 Booker Prize was announced on Tuesday. The list includes previous Booker Prize winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart, and Elizabeth Strout, with her second appearance on the shortlist, which features authors representing four countries: England, Scotland, Jamaica, and the US.

This year’s jury is chaired by classicist and writer Mary Beard. The other members are educator Raymond Antrobus; musician and writer Jarvis Cocker; journalist and critic Rebecca Liu; and Booker Prize-shortlisted novelist Patricia Lockwood.

The shortlist spans a range of genres from dystopian fiction to contemporary realism, and campus satire to historical fiction. According to Beard: “These novels range from the hilarious to the discomfiting, from the frighteningly strange to the alarmingly domestic, from the powerfully shocking to the intriguingly understated. In them, we meet characters from different countries and different centuries, created by authors 40 years apart, new talent and well-known favourites. This is writing at its best. There’s plenty to enjoy, some blissful escapism and prose to die for (‘I just wish I could have written that’ kept going through my mind). But there is also plenty here to change the way we see the world, to surprise us and to challenge our certainties.”

item.title: India rejects Organisation of Islamic Cooperation remarks on J&K as ‘unwarranted’
item.description: The bloc had stated that it was committed to supporting the ‘inalienable right of the Kashmiri people to self-determination’.
item.content:encoded:
India on Wednesday categorically rejected what it described as “unwarranted and factually incorrect references” to the country in a joint statement issued by the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation Contact Group on Jammu and Kashmir.

The OIC has 57 member states, most of them Muslim-majority countries and claims to represent the “collective voice of the Muslim world”. Pakistan, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Azerbaijan and Niger are part of the bloc.

The group held a meeting on Tuesday in New York on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. It stated that it was committed to supporting the “inalienable right of the Kashmiri people to self-determination”.

The organisation’s Secretary-General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed expressed concern about the “humanitarian, human rights and security situation” in Jammu and Kashmir, read the statement.

It added that he had also called for “respect for its international status” and the “revocation of the unilateral and illegal measures” taken since 2019, in an apparent reference to the abrogation of Article 370 of the Constitution.

item.title: Orangutans in Odisha signal India is emerging as a destination for illegal primate pet trade
item.description: Experts say most of these animals are caught in the wild, which means separating them their mothers, raising serious welfare concerns.
item.content:encoded:
Recently, pictures and videos of five orangutan babies in a forest in Odisha, thousands of miles from their real home, were plastered across many screens. As authorities investigate the antecedents of the critically endangered animals and discuss their future, one thing is becoming increasingly clear: international wildlife trafficking is widening its reach, and India is emerging as a destination.

Keeping exotic animals and birds as pets, is not new in India. Non-native parrots have long dominated the scene. But keeping them legally involves navigating a complex set of legal procedures.

The repertoire of species illegally reaching Indian shores, however, has expanded significantly in recent years.

Primates are the new parrots. Gibbons, lemurs, marmosets and macaques, once difficult to find outside their native ranges, are increasingly turning up in seizures linked to the illegal pet trade.

Primates are a group of mammals that includes humans, apes, monkeys, lemurs and lorises, generally characterised by grasping hands and feet, forward-facing eyes and relatively large brains.

The seizure of an orangutan from an apartment bathroom in Mumbai in 2024, a Tamil actor’s pet Lar gibbon, and the controversy over two lemurs at Vantara highlight the emerging trade.

item.title: Fiction: Abandoned near the border, Nimki is taken in by the Senguptas to work as their maid
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Beyond Our Births’, by Antara Mukherjee.
item.content:encoded:
For the next few years, Nimki continued to live as an outsider without knowing how she had landed with the Senguptas. Every time she tried asking, they led her into a discussion about the dinner that had to be cooked or her doll that needed a bath. It had become all too obvious that they kept from her a secret that was about her. All she knew was that she was born in the month of September, on a stormy Sunday night, when a brown cow had mooed. However, despite these precise details, she was told that her age was still a mystery. In fact, this had been a much-debated topic before the Senguptas could mutually agree upon an age for her. Nimki had therefore understood early on that this was a family that discussed more and decided less.

These discussions, at the same time, had confirmed her fears. She was born to poor parents. She had overheard that children with humble beginnings often had stunted growth and looked much younger. item.title: How John Coltrane is my bridge between two loves – jazz and Carnatic music
item.description: There is something distinctly Indian about his approach to modal jazz.
item.content:encoded:
The first time I heard John Coltrane was 25 years ago, and I didn’t even realise I was listening to him. He was one of two saxophonists on the Miles Davis album Kind of Blue, and I couldn’t tell them apart. A few more listens made the difference between Coltrane’s tenor and “Cannonball” Adderley’s alto clear to the ear, though I still knew nothing about either man.

Once I could tell the two saxophone sounds apart, I noticed the tenor solos literally took off, and Coltrane’s lack of patience made me very curious about him. I was into a lot of musicians in those years, and few have survived in my collection. Even fewer are the ones I start my day with. Coltrane is the only one I am still trying to understand.

item.title: Meghalaya: Eight United Democratic Party MLAs join ally BJP
item.description: The Bharatiya Janata Party and the United Democratic Party are part of the state’s ruling coalition.
item.content:encoded:
Eight MLAs of the United Democratic Party in Meghalaya joined the Bharatiya Janata Party on Wednesday.

This took the BJP’s tally in the 60-member Assembly to 10 from two, making it the second-largest party in the House. The United Democratic Party is left with four legislators. Chief Minister Conrad Sangma-led National People’s Party is the largest party with 33 MLAs.

The United Democratic Party and the National People’s Party are part of the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance at the national level. The three parties are also part of the ruling Meghalaya Democratic Alliance in the state.

The MLAs who joined the BJP are Lahkmen Rymbui, Pius Marwein, Kyrmen Shylla, Mayralborn Syiem, Matthew Kurbah, Ollan Singh Suin, Balajied Kupar Synrem and Synshar Lyngdoh Thabah.

They were inducted into the Hindutva party in Delhi in the presence of Union minister Kiren Rijiju.

Rijiju said that the eight legislators joining the BJP, from an ally, will “further strengthen” the Sangma government. It will lead to better coordination, “more understanding” and help improve efforts to develop Meghalaya, the BJP leader said.

The proceedings involved the conglomerate’s flagship company Adani Enterprises, and subsidiaries Adani Total Gas, Adani Green, Adani Energy Solutions, formerly known as Adani Transmission, and AWL Agri Business Limited, which was previously named Adani Wilmar.

The market regulator had examined allegations pertaining to non-disclosure of alleged related-party transactions and problems of corporate governance that Hindenburg had claimed. On Wednesday, The Indian Express reported that some of the concerns about the conduct of the exercise had also come from within the Election Commission.

Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi formally objected at least 14 times in the past 10 months to decisions related to the SIR, saying that some had been taken without their knowledge, the newspaper reported.

Unlike with the previous updates to the electoral rolls, to be included in the revised lists this time, voters need to show that they or their parents are present on the 2002 voter lists. That was when the last SIR was conducted.

At that time, the poll panel had taken double the time to revise the lists.

item.title: This book traces the restoration and transformation of Delhi’s Sunder Nursery and its surroundings
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Gardens Within a Garden: Sunder Nursery, New Delhi’, edited by Geeta Wahi Dua and Archana Saad Akhtar.
item.content:encoded:
The green space of New York is designed on an altogether different scale and enclosure. The permanent visibility of the city, its vibrancy of size and height, is forever present in Manhattan’s many and varied forms of landscape. In a place of formidable urban density, the landscape always appears as precious space held in architectural captivity – sometimes a square of leafy trees on stone paving surrounded by apartment blocks, sometimes a 50th-floor balcony with a terrace garden. New York is amply endowed with as much designed open space as accidental reveals. In one such instance, a small graveyard belonging to an 18th-century Greek Orthodox church sits along one of the busiest high-rise streets of lower Manhattan. The frenzy of the financial district is hard to miss in a part of town where Wall Street bankers spend much of the day scurrying between the office and the stock exchange. In an area so overbuilt, the old churchyard provides much-needed relief. As its garden is open to the public, many traders can be seen sitting for lunch in the high grass overlooked by skyscrapers. item.title: Another court grants ‘rights’ to an Indian river but that doesn’t address our disconnect from nature
item.description: Legal personhood for nature should recognise and help reimagine our interconnected relationship with the world we live in.
item.content:encoded:
On July 23, noting that “rivers can’t be polluted in the name of religion”, the Madras High Court recognised the rights of the Tamirabarani River as a juristic person – a non-human legal entity that has the capacity to hold rights and duties just like a human being.

This is the sixth pronouncement in India to grant legal personhood to an element of nature, including to Ganga and Yamuna, Sukhna lake, and animals in general.

These developments are part of a growing international movement towards recognising the “rights of nature”. In 2019, the Dhaka High Court recognised all rivers in Bangladesh as holding legal rights of a living entity. There have also been legal and constitutional developments towards this in Bolivia and Ecuador, among other places.

But this raises a range of scientific, ethical and institutional questions: What rights might a river have? What would constitute a violation of a river’s rights? How can these rights be put into practice within existing governance structures? Are legal rights an adequate framework for protecting nature?

These questions are particularly important in South Asia. Long before Western legal systems began accepting arguments around the rights of nature, social movements and peoples’ worldviews across the region had articulated relationships of respect, reverence and responsibility...

item.title: ‘Illegal, arbitrary’: Why experts say detention regime in Bengal has fewer safeguards than Assam
item.description: The BJP government in the state has adopted a process that allows the police to be ‘judge, jury and executioner of citizenship’ all at once, they said.

item.title: How lunch and sleep pressure can cause the ‘3pm slump’
item.description: A better way to push back against the afternoon dip is using natural light, or even taking a short nap.
item.content:encoded:
You’ve just finished eating lunch and you’re back at your desk, ready to dive into the rest of the day’s work. Yet by 3pm, you find your eyes starting to droop. Before long, the only thing you can think about is how much you’d like to take a nap.

The “afternoon slump” (also sometimes called the “3pm slump”) is a common experience. It’s that distinct drop in energy that tends to occur in the mid-afternoon hours.

While it’s tempting to blame this sudden urge to snooze on what you’ve eaten for lunch, this alone can’t take the blame. The afternoon slump is actually caused by several distinct biological pressures beginning to converge.

One part of the explanation begins long before lunch. From the moment we wake up, our drive to sleep gradually increases. Adenosine – an organic compound involved in regulating sleep and wakefulness – accumulates in the brain while we’re awake, contributing to our gradual need to sleep, referred to as “sleep pressure”.

Yet the reason we do not simply become progressively sleepier from breakfast onwards is because another system is working alongside it. Our circadian clock, which controls our body’s sleep-wake system, generates a changing drive for wakefulness across the day.

The photograph showed Srishti Gupta, a 28-year-old artist, addressing a group of women, who were listening attentively. Gupta used to run basic literacy classes for the women of Shahbad Dairy, Kumari recalled.

A few steps away from this exhibit, scraps carrying children’s messages for Gupta adorned a sheet of sky-blue chart paper that hung from a string. “Miss you Srishti didi,” many of the messages read, using the Hindi word for elder sister as a mark of respect. Some of the children told Scroll that Gupta besides teaching them art also helped them revise their school lessons.

item.title: A new book examines how socially entrenched food biases in India can endanger health
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Meat of the Matter: How the Politics of Food Shapes Our Health’, by Sylvia Karpagam.
item.content:encoded:
The fact that entrenched vegetarianism distances itself not just from meat, but also the meat-eater in physical as well as social ways, is largely ignored. That these social ways translate into the shameful practices of discrimination, denial, neglect, negligence, humiliation and untouchability is never recognised and acknowledged in these “simple” discourses. Separate plates, separate counters, separate kitchens, separate sinks and, indeed, separate cutlery, are all proof that untouchability is alive and well among Indians. What starts as not wanting to sit beside a meat-eater then transforms into them not being allowed into classrooms, not being allowed into educational institutions, and not being allowed to access education itself. “Legitimised” exclusion from all public and private spaces is precisely how the caste system operates. Ultimately, the entitled belief that vegetarians are superior is enough to demand that meat-eaters be kept away from them and perpetuates and sustains casteism in all its virulent forms.

In reality, these stereotypical behaviours are neither simple nor innocent because they have far-reaching consequences. The myth of India’s vegetarianism adeptly subsumes and erases nutritious and diverse cultures and traditions. item.title: Who is Durga’s mother? Assam elephant’s transfer to TN temple raises troubling legal questions
item.description: Indian law accords elephants the highest protection. But a contradiction allows the national heritage animal to be held in private captivity.
item.content:encoded:
India gives elephants its highest level of wildlife protection and reveres them culturally and religiously. Why, then, do we continue to allow them to be owned and to spend their entire lives in captivity?

Earlier this month, Durga, a five-year-old elephant, was transported from Assam to the Meenakshi Amman Temple in Madurai, nearly 3,000 km away.

Her transfer has brought into sharp focus an old contradiction in Indian wildlife law – and raised a new and particularly troubling set of questions about how this young animal came into private custody.

The owned elephant

The elephant is a Schedule I animal under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, receiving the highest level of statutory protection, and is India’s National Heritage Animal. Yet a sub-category of elephants – those already in private ownership before 1972, and their documented, captive-born descendants – can be owned, transferred and kept in captivity for the whole of their lives, six decades on.

The elaborate regulatory framework that has developed around this category seeks to govern captivity without ever questioning it. This produces an obvious contradiction: the same species that the law protects in the wild can become the legal property of a human being outside it.

item.title: Women were excluded from decades of scientific studies based on a mistaken assumption
item.description: These practices have continued to inform, perhaps mistakenly, our understanding of issues ranging from athletic performance to the benefits of exercise.
item.content:encoded:
What if much of what we thought we knew about women’s health and fitness was suddenly called into question?

Researchers in many fields of science, including my area of exercise physiology, are facing this scenario, after generations of research that either left out women participants altogether or significantly reduced their numbers in countless experiments.

These practices have continued to inform, perhaps mistakenly, our understanding of issues ranging from athletic performance to the benefits of exercise, where we have been left to presume it was OK to generalise results from testing men as if they applied to women and men equally.

These are not just old studies from back in the day when women were routinely excluded from many arenas. These are also studies from the past 20 years, when many people thought research was finally catching up.

Menstruation, birth control

Leaving women out of scientific studies has largely been the result of uncertainty over how to account for potential fluctuations related to menstruation or hormonal birth control.

Not knowing how or whether these factors might affect, for example, muscle function, researchers simply included fewer women in their research, or didn’t include them at all, based on assumptions that turned out to be incorrect.

item.title: ‘Exotic’ pets are a growing health risk for humans and wildlife
item.description: Poor traceability, inadequate surveillance and close human-animal contact can make viral and bacterial spillovers difficult to detect.
item.content:encoded:
Mumbai-based veterinarian Dr Rina Dev was hospitalised for four days recently with a lung infection. “I hope it’s not something from the parrots I was treating,” she told Mongabay-India after being discharged from the hospital. Dr Dev is an avian and exotic animal veterinarian who works closely with the forest department to treat imported and seized exotic animals involved in the wildlife trade.

Her concerns are valid. Avian chlamydiosis, or psittacosis, is caused by the bacterium Chlamydia psittaci and is a common infection among people who handle birds, earning it the nickname “bird handler’s disease”.

A 2024 case from India describes a man contracting the infection after exposure to his pet parrot. In 1994, customs officers in Belgium contracted chlamydiosis after being exposed to infected parakeets. Multiple such documented cases link wildlife trade to human infection.

A comprehensive review of psittacosis by the ICAR-Indian Veterinary Research Institute in 2021 describes avian chlamydiosis as a “neglected disease” with “critical zoonotic potential”.

Pet trade link to zoonosis

Zoonoses, or zoonotic diseases, entered the ordinary Indian’s wellness lexicon when the Covid-19 pandemic exposed how pathogens can jump from animals to humans, causing serious medical consequences and, in some cases, a pandemic that can literally bring the world to a standstill.

item.title: ‘I learn not to carry the hurt / like a loaded gun’: These poems are diverse manifestations of home
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Call Me Home’, by Harman Kaur.
item.content:encoded:
My Mother’s Loss

When I ask my mother what she misses the most about
Panjab, she says to me

I cry, laugh, and get angry in my maa boli.
These emotions roll off my tongue in the
language that is natural to me. Here, my feelings
must be translated. In Panjab, they are understood.

I miss being understood.

And I realise my people have been lost in translation.


My Father’s Dilemma

One foot is in Panjab
planted deep in soil
roots attached to the khet
like kanak

the other here
in a new country
scraping against
concrete roads

no wonder I keep falling down:
life won’t let me keep balance.


Maapeh

You worked the soil
of a new country

sun beating down on
broken backs and
dirt stuck in fingernails

planted seeds that cost
everything you had

and from this
I harvested my dreams.


Numb

There is no doubt about it:
It is easier to think of anything but the grief,
to drift in a constant state of numbness.

The cuts keep coming, but I no longer feel them.
I wear my scars like badges, battle-worn,
yet, truth be told,
I do not remember when they formed – or how.

The anaesthesia will fade, eventually,
but healing means confronting the pain.

And who wants to walk down the street,
only to come face to face with their mistakes?


Chekov’s Gun

In another lifetime,

I learn not to carry the hurt
like a loaded gun.

In another lifetime,

you are bulletproof.

Italy is preparing to ban burqas and niqabs in schools and limit the number of foreign students in each class, Reuters quoted Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni as saying on Sunday.

The proposed measures would also require parents of foreign students facing “serious difficulties integrating into the school system” to attend Italian language classes, Meloni said.

The prime minister announced the measures at an annual gathering of the youth wing of her right-wing Brothers of Italy party in Rome.

Her party is expected to face a challenge in the 2027 general election from the National Future party, which has taken a harder line on immigration, Al Jazeera reported. Immigration is expected to be a key topic in the polls.

Neither burqas or niqabs are expressly banned in Italy, but a 1975 law prohibits the use of helmets or garments that make identification difficult without a justified reason.

A 2008 ruling clarified that full-face coverings may be worn for religious or cultural reasons if the face is revealed when identity verification is required.

Students who are not Italian citizens account for 11.6% of those enrolled in Italian schools, or nearly 12 in 100, Reuters quoted data by Fondazione ISMU research institute as saying.

item.title: Canada’s overqualified immigrants suffer at work but companies pay the price too
item.description: Managers cannot fix broader systemic causes but can influence what happens once an overqualified immigrant is on the job.
item.content:encoded:
Canada actively recruits highly educated and skilled immigrants through programs, yet many of these immigrants struggle to find work matching their skills and experience.

Nearly one in three immigrants with a post-secondary education report that they are overqualified for their jobs. Statistics Canada data from 2024 and 2025 puts the figure at 33%, compared with 19% among Canadian-born workers.

Much of the discourse around this issue has focused, understandably, on why skilled immigrants end up in jobs below their qualifications. Their foreign credentials, skills and experience are often undervalued, particularly when they come from non-OECD countries, while employers tend to favour candidates with Canadian experience.

These are critical issues, and efforts to address them must continue. But less attention has been paid to why this mismatch is not only a problem for employees, but also for employers, and what employers can do when an overqualified immigrant is already on the job.

item.title: Why it is important to teach students what AI cannot do when it comes to writing
item.description: Students should be taught to distinguish AI’s pattern recognition skills from its inability to inhabit human perspectives and authentically express itself.
item.content:encoded:
It’s disconcerting to envision human thought becoming redundant or deemed inferior due to advancements in artificial intelligence. But for all its ills, AI cannot be ignored or wished away. It’s here to stay, and I want my students to understand the stakes of becoming too reliant on this technology.

I can’t blame them for wondering why they should dedicate so much time and effort to honing their writing and critical thinking skills if large language models appear to do a passable job.

Yet this situation has major implications for culture and societies.

It’s easy to envision a future where AI dependency leads to intellectual conformity and the erosion of critical thinking. Researchers are already documenting these effects, which threaten to render the hard work of wrestling with ideas a lost art.

This is why I think it’s critical for educators to confront AI head-on. The key, I believe, is teaching students to distinguish AI’s pattern recognition skills from its inability to daydream, inhabit human perspectives and authentically express itself.

item.title: ‘Dechoma and the Women of Mahe’: This novel maps girlhood between beauty and its absence

item.title: ‘The act of writing is un-citizenly’: Amit Chaudhuri talks about his new novel, ‘Château Rouge’
item.description: ‘The primary attachment of a writer is to explore a domain of freedom which verges on the irresponsible, the indifferent, the absurd.’
item.content:encoded:
In Amit Chaudhuri’s ninth novel, Château Rouge, an Indian writer arriving in Paris for a fellowship finds himself in a sublet apartment in Château Rouge, a dense, multicultural quarter sometimes called “Little Africa.” It is not the storied Paris of “Proust’s house and Baldwin’s digs,” of monuments and cafes, nor does it resemble the kind of Parisian grime popularised across the literature and myth around the city. item.title: How AI could influence our understanding of mathematics: A computer scientist-novelist’s reflections
item.description: Perhaps the new age of mathematics will favour a mind that delights in speculation, leaps of the imagination and a deep sense of aesthetics.
item.content:encoded:
On September 8, OpenAI claimed it had solved the Navier-Stokes problem. “The question of whether smooth three-dimensional fluid motion can break down has remained unresolved for roughly 90 years,” Open AI said. It put 10,000 AI agents to work on it and the task took 88 hours. What might this mean for how we “do” mathematics?


It is not really clear how mathematicians chose to become mathematicians. After all, there are no “creative mathematics” courses for the budding mathematician the way there are “creative writing” courses for the budding storyteller or poet. There are no celebrity mathematicians to crush on (let’s ignore Brian Cox). Mathematics books for children have ominous reassurances of just how fun, just how easy, just how natural the subject is; this is in direct contradiction with the student’s own experience. So either the books are lying or the student is a duffer. Frankly, given the circumstances, it is a wonder anyone becomes a mathematician.

Though we do not know how mathematicians are made, we do know what mathematicians do after they become professional mathematicians. They work on proofs. That’s really it. They prove things day in and day out, and if they have time left to spare or if their lunch money depends...

item.title: ‘White Elephant’: Jeyamohan’s excellent novel is backed by an equally excellent translation
item.description: Set in the 19th century, Jeyamohan brings to life the Dalit protests at the Madras Ice House as vividly as the horrors of the 1876 famine.
item.content:encoded:
On Chennai’s Kamaraja Salai, just off Marina Beach, stands a large circular building now known as Vivekanandar Illam, after Swami Vivekananda, who stayed here for a while. It’s a city landmark, but relatively few people know of the building’s blood-soaked past, its connections to Chennai’s colonial history as well as to caste politics, commercialism – and the sheer ruthlessness and greed of those who would not let anything come in the way of their ambition for power and wealth. Till 1880, this edifice was the Ice House at Madras, built in 1842 by American merchant-businessman Frederic Tudor to store ice shipped from the lakes and ponds of New England.

The Ice House and the famine

item.title: Ramachandra Guha: India needs fearless civil liberties activists more than ever

I work mostly by myself, and have resisted joining alumni associations and WhatsApp groups. I am, in other words, broadly of the same mind as Groucho Marx, who famously said that he would never join a club which would have him as a member.

Yet for a few brief years in Delhi in the 1980s, I associated myself with the People’s Union for Democratic Rights, a citizens group that sought to hold the Indian State to account for the varied crimes it committed against Indian citizens. I attended the PUDR’s Saturday meetings at the Triveni Kala Sangam, paid a very modest amount from my stipend to help fund its reports, and on one occasion even joined a fact-finding group it had organised.

item.title: ‘I’m not Mr Political’: Ed Sheeran’s stance has larger implications, explains an ethicist
item.description: The musician has allowed Macklemore’s political views to be removed at the behest of another party acting in its own political interest, thereby taking sides.
item.content:encoded:
Headlines this week have been inundated with news of artist Macklemore being dropped from Ed Sheeran’s Loop tour, following Macklemore’s onstage calls to “free Palestine”.

The rap artist said Robert Kraft, owner of New England Patriots and the Gillette Stadium, barred him from playing in his stadium, and rallied other stadiums to join the boycott.

In response, Sheeran’s remaining support acts also withdrew. Sheeran has attempted to distance himself from the decision, suggesting it was the promoter’s and not his. He has taken an “apolitical” stance, referring back to his history of avoiding public political statements.

But the resulting condemnation from fans and commentators suggests forcing neutrality in such situations isn’t straightforward.

What does it mean to be ‘apolitical’?

Politics isn’t limited to government. In a more general sense, it refers to the relationships of power in society and between members of society, and efforts to change them.

This seems to be what Ed Sheeran’s recent statements are reaching for. item.title: What is fascism in the present? Two recent books attempt to diagnose these conditions
item.description: How can fascism in the present help explain contemporary technological, social and political dynamics? Two recent books attempt to diagnose these conditions.
item.content:encoded:
“A moment of reckoning has arrived for the West,” reads a recent recruitment ad for Palantir, a Silicon Valley firm that increasingly provides data-driven “intelligence” for intelligence, police and military agencies – as well as blue-chip corporations and non-profits. “On the factory floor, in the operating room, across the battlefield,” the ad intones, “we build to dominate.”

How do we make sense of this convergence between advanced technologies and unapologetic violence, between “rational” AI and a primordial view of the world that seems to revert to a language of blood and soil, friends and enemies, “us” and “them”? In op-eds, talk shows, and political analyses, a single word has risen to prominence: fascism.

As a term, “fascism” is highly provocative, but seemingly untimely. It conjures up powerful images of jackbooted throngs of followers repeating chants and salutes, visions of black-lettered and blood-red banners. Yet these images are typically associated with political orders from a century ago in interwar Europe, a dusty relic from a previous age where “evil” was identified and annihilated.

item.title: Snakebite treatment: Promising research on nanobody antivenoms
item.description: A shared set of nanobodies could potentially be combined and adapted for different geographical regions.
item.content:encoded:
Every year, between 80,000 and 140,000 people die from snakebites worldwide. Hundreds of thousands more are left with amputated limbs or permanent disabilities.

India accounts for roughly half of these deaths, with around 58,000 people dying from snakebites each year. Many of the victims are farmers, labourers and children in rural communities, bitten while working in the fields or walking home after dark.

Yet the basic way we treat snakebite has changed little in more than a century. Traditional antivenom is made using horses: they are injected with small doses of snake venom, prompting their immune systems to produce antibodies. Blood is then collected from the horse and processed to make the antivenom.

This type of antivenom has saved countless lives, but it has drawbacks. The antivenom can vary from batch to batch, cause severe allergic reactions and is expensive to produce.

It can also offer limited protection. For example, in India, antivenom is mainly made using venoms from four snake species known as the “big four”: the Indian spectacled cobra, common krait, Russell’s viper, and saw-scaled viper. But these antivenoms do not always work well against venoms from other snake species, or populations of the same snake species, found across the country.

item.title: How dreaded dacoit Phoolan Devi became an irresistible legend
item.description: To revisit the bandit’s intensely eventful life is to be reminded of all that was done to her – and all that she refused to ignore.
item.content:encoded:
It’s hard to imagine a time when Phoolan Devi was not an icon.

Ever since news spread in the early 1980s about the “Bandit Queen”, the only woman dacoit in the Chambal Valley, Phoolan has made the headlines and fired the imagination of writers and filmmakers.

In addition to her own autobiography, there are at least three biographies of Phoolan, a graphic novel and a biopic.

Interest in the outlaw who roamed the Chambal valley in a khaki police uniform, a double sash of bullets around her chest and a crimson-red cloth around her forehead while looting villages and avenging attacks by members of the dominant castes has been rekindled by the premiere in Toronto on September 16 of a movie by Richie Mehta titled Phoolan.

item.title: ‘The Yellow Metaphor’: Jiban Narah’s poetry signifies luminous precarity through the yellow colour
item.description: Anindita Kar’s translation does not simply transpose language but preserves the tonal grain and ecological timbre of Narah’s poetry.
item.content:encoded:
Jiban Narah’s collection of Assamese lyrics, The Yellow Metaphor, has been translated into English by Anindita Kar. His decades-long practice has given him consummate mastery and imaginative control over the lyric form.

The metaphors and symbols in his poetic representation serve as powerful devices to unearth hidden emotional and intellectual connections. Together, they expand across memories, ecology and contemporary politics. His lyrics emerge from a chemistry of folk inheritance, intuitive perception of the elemental forces, and a sharp insight into their workings. We see his intuitive power at its best to evoke sensual nuances out of the classic elements of the earth – river, rain, flora and fauna, paddy fields, sunshine, moonlight.

A distinct articulation

Kar’s translation penetrates deeply into Narah’s poetic voice, capturing its conversational idiom, childhood memories, private emotions, musical flow of diction and rhythms shaped by the cross-cultural milieu of Assam. Her translation does not merely find verbal equivalents or transfer the content into the target language. Instead, it preserves subtle nuances of tone, reinforcing the ecological ethos. What, thus, emerges in English is not an approximation but an afterlife – a focused exploration of themes rooted in the riparian landscape and collective memory.

At least 31 persons were killed and more than 100 injured in an alleged militant attack at a police headquarters in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Friday, AFP quoted an unidentified police officer as saying on Saturday.

A car allegedly packed with explosives rammed into the entrance of a mosque inside the police compound in Kohat town on Friday afternoon, BBC reported. Friday prayers were underway at the time.

Gun fight between the suspected militants and police officers continued till Saturday morning, AFP reported.

A local militant group, Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, a faction linked to Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, has claimed responsibility for the attack, the news agency reported.

Of those killed in the “militant attack and suicide bombing” incident, 16 were police personnel, the officer said.

“An exchange of fire with them has been ongoing since late last night,” the news agency quoted the officer as saying. “Their exact number remains unclear.”

The Old Police Lines complex serves as the district police headquarters and houses offices of Pakistan’s Counter Terrorism Department, Special Branch and other police units.

Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the attack on Friday evening and expressed “deep sorrow and regret” over the injuries caused by the blast, the news agency reported.

item.title: Why India resisted the Caribbean diaspora’s attempts to return home
item.description: A community shaped by indentureship found its dream of returning home colliding with the upheaval of Partition.
item.content:encoded:
Almost as soon as Anand Mohan Sahay took charge as India’s commissioner in the British colony of Trinidad in 1950, he began receiving Indian-origin visitors seeking repatriation to India. They were either former indentured labourers or their descendants.

“Some of them are persons of moderately independent means and propose to set up some small trade to maintain themselves for the rest of their lives in India,” Sahay wrote in a December 1950 letter to Foreign Secretary Subimal Dutt. He added that, in some cases, younger, well-off people were willing to financially support parents who wished to die in the land of their birth.

After the indentured labour system was abolished in the Caribbean in 1917, some Indians decided to move to India, while the majority remained in the West Indies. By the time India attained independence in 1947, Trinidad and British Guiana (now Guyana) had more than 3 lakh people of Indian origin. In the late 1940s and early 1950s, Indians in the Caribbean loosely organised a “Back to India” movement, appealing to both the British colonial authorities and the Indian government.
